identification.summary: Storm-0230 is a Microsoft 'group in development' designation that Malpedia records as a Wizard Spider alias [S3]; Microsoft's naming mapping [S1] could not be re-verified in this check. MITRE describes Wizard Spider as a Russia-based, financially motivated threat group originally known for creating and deploying TrickBot since at least 2016 [S2]. Malpedia lists Storm-0230 among Wizard Spider aliases together with DEV-0193, GOLD BLACKBURN, TEMP.MixMaster, Trickbot LLC and UNC2053 [S3]. Wizard Spider operated, or was closely tied to, the Ryuk and Conti ransomware operations [S5][S8].
identification.firstObserved: TrickBot activity since at least 2016 per MITRE [S2]; Wizard Spider is described as emerging in 2016 from the Dyre banking trojan [S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-0230 (Group in development) [S1]. The 'Conti Team 1' label seen in earlier drafts could not be confirmed by independent search and is not asserted here; no source found explicitly documents the Storm-0230 to Conti mapping beyond Microsoft's mapping file and Malpedia [S1][S3]. Leaked Conti chats are described as referring to internal teams of unclear membership; Black Basta is reported as formerly 'Conti Team Three' [S9]. Do not equate Storm-0230 with the whole Wizard Spider/Conti ecosystem or with FIN12: Mandiant is reported to have seen FIN12 deploy Conti only once and to be unsure whether FIN12 is core developer or affiliate [S3][S8].

attribution.sponsor: Financially motivated Russia-based cybercrime group; no state sponsor established in the cited sources [S2]. The US Treasury is reported to have tied current TrickBot members to Russian intelligence services based on 2020 activity [S5]. A search summary of Trellix's Conti-leaks analysis (page not opened, not a listed source) mentions a single leaked-chat claim linking the Conti leader to the FSB; treat as unverified.
attribution.confidence: Assessments belong to the named parties: MITRE assesses Wizard Spider as Russia-based and financially motivated [S2]; the US and UK sanctioned individuals for TrickBot, Ryuk and Conti activity in February 2023 [S5]; German police reportedly confirmed a leaker's identification of the Conti leader 'Stern' in 2025 [S6]. Mandiant is reported to have high confidence that Conti and TrickBot management and development staff are closely aligned [S8].
attribution.basis: Sanctions and indictments (reported via press coverage, primary Treasury/DOJ documents not opened) [S5]; leaked internal Conti chats analysed by KELA and others [S4]; MITRE ATT&CK group profile [S2]; Microsoft naming mapping [S1].

objectives: Financial gain through ransomware extortion and the TrickBot botnet ecosystem [S2][S5]. Conti reportedly paid developers a monthly wage rather than the percentage model of most ransomware groups [S9].

sectors: Healthcare (FIN12 overlap, Mandiant, unconfirmed as same cluster) [S8]
Broad cross-sector victims of Conti ransomware [S7]
regions: Global; the FBI is reported to have estimated over 1,000 Conti victims and payouts exceeding $150 million as of January 2022 [S7]
targeting.notes: Targeting information is for the Conti/Wizard Spider ecosystem and may not be specific to the Storm-0230 designation [S1][S7].

capabilities.summary: TrickBot botnet and loader ecosystem, Ryuk and Conti ransomware, with BazarLoader and Cobalt Strike named as principal tools in the leaked Conti chats (Forescout analysis, via search summary) [S2][S5][S4]. Conti reportedly absorbed the TrickBot operation in early 2022 with a plan to replace TrickBot with BazarBackdoor [S8]. Leaked chats show functional teams including hackers, coders, testers, crypters, reverse engineers, OSINT specialists, negotiators, IT support and HR [S4]. Analysis of the leaks and on-chain data suggests Conti is a rebrand of Ryuk [S10].

campaigns.name: TrickBot emerges
campaigns.summary: Wizard Spider is described as emerging in 2016 from the Dyre banking trojan, with MITRE dating TrickBot activity to at least 2016.

campaigns.name: Conti chats leaked
campaigns.summary: A suspected Ukrainian researcher released internal Conti chats after the group backed Russia's invasion of Ukraine; the chats exposed team structure and links to Ryuk and TrickBot.

campaigns.name: Costa Rica government attacks
campaigns.summary: Conti claimed attacks on Costa Rican government agencies including the Finance Ministry; the president declared a national cybersecurity emergency in May 2022 and the government said it would not pay the ransom. Start date is reported as April 12 or April 18 by different outlets.

campaigns.name: Conti brand shut down
campaigns.summary: Conti infrastructure including its site, negotiation service and chat rooms was reported shut down or reset; AdvIntel judged the brand was being retired so the group could splinter into separate teams.

campaigns.name: US-UK sanctions
campaigns.summary: The US and UK sanctioned seven Russian nationals tied to TrickBot, Ryuk and Conti, including Vitaly Kovalev; a later round sanctioned further individuals (date not confirmed in sources read).

campaigns.name: GangExposed leaks
campaigns.summary: A leaker calling himself GangExposed named Conti leader 'Stern' as Vitaly Nikolaevich Kovalev; German police reportedly later confirmed the identity.

diamond.adversary: Russia-based cybercrime organisation (Wizard Spider/Conti), with named individuals sanctioned in 2023 [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: TrickBot, BazarLoader, Cobalt Strike, Ryuk and Conti ransomware [S2][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Botnet and loader infrastructure, ransomware leak site and negotiation service, shut down or reset in May 2022 [S9]; specific infrastructure not detailed in sources read.
diamond.victim: Broad cross-sector, including Costa Rican government agencies and over 1,000 reported victims by January 2022 [S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financially motivated criminal enterprise; the group's public support for Russia in 2022 triggered the leaks [S4]; reported Treasury statement of intelligence-service ties [S5], plus an unverified leaked-chat claim (see gaps).
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks reachable by phishing-delivered loaders and later ransomware deployment [S4]; details not confirmed in sources read.

gaps: No source found defines any Conti sub-team or states which activity Storm-0230 covers; the mapping relies on Malpedia [S3] and Microsoft's mapping file [S1], and other vendors list Periwinkle Tempest as Microsoft's current Wizard Spider name.

Primary documents not opened: Microsoft mapping rationale, US Treasury/OFAC and DOJ releases, UK FCDO sanctions text, Mandiant FIN12/UNC2053 reports, CrowdStrike WIZARD SPIDER update, and the MITRE G0102 page (all fetches failed on network errors; MITRE content taken from search summaries).
FIN12 and UNC2053 relationships to Wizard Spider are only secondary-sourced and Mandiant's own assessment is reported as uncertain [S8].
Successor links (Black Basta, Royal, BlackByte, Karakurt, Quantum/BumbleBee) are described as overlaps in tooling, infrastructure and personnel, not confirmed succession [S9][S10].
Current (2024-2026) Storm-0230 activity is not documented in sources found.
Alleged Russian intelligence ties are press-reported (Treasury statement via S5) or from a single leaked chat (Trellix, not opened) and are unverified.
Publication dates for S8 (GovInfoSecurity) and S10 (TRM Labs) were not visible in search results and are estimated from context; verify.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is enterprise Windows networks, domain controllers, backups and public-sector systems that ransomware can disrupt, as shown by the Costa Rica emergency [S7]. STEP 2: The ecosystem is a criminal enterprise with specialised teams, so its capacity regenerates after brand shutdowns and sanctions [S4][S9]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is loader or botnet access (TrickBot, BazarLoader), Cobalt Strike hands-on activity, then ransomware and data-theft extortion [S2][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued ransomware and extortion against government and critical-service organisations under changing brand names. MDCOA is a ransomware or wiper-like event against a DoD-supporting contractor or allied government timed to a geopolitical crisis, noting the group's 2022 political alignment [S4][S7]. Candidate indicators: Cobalt Strike beacons, BazarLoader or TrickBot detections, and mass credential or backup access prior to encryption [S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track ransomware brand changes and map them to underlying team overlaps instead of relying on names [S9]. (2) Authorities: criminal sanctions and indictments constrain payments and dealings with named individuals [S5]; consult legal and law-enforcement channels before any engagement. (3) Mission assurance: protect backups and recovery paths for mission-critical government and contractor systems given the Costa Rica precedent [S7]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3, the DIB CS program and allied partners; handle attribution claims of Russian intelligence ties cautiously [S5].
